However, in our Orthopaedics business, we will expect at least a step up of 200 basis points from the 11.5. At least 13.5, hopefully getting towards 14. The key drivers behind that are twofold. The first of which is obviously operational leverage coming through growing our top line and recovery in our US Orthopaedics business, as we've already talked about.
The second one, which of course is a big chunk of that will also come from savings, particularly the closure of the 4 manufacturing units that supported that business and the benefits those savings coming through in the H2 of the year. 2 big levers on Orthopaedics to deliver that 200 basis points of margin expansion, operational leverage, and manufacturing cost savings.
Robert Davies
Analyst, Morgan Stanley
Morning. Robert Davies from Morgan Stanley. 2 questions. 1 was just on the headcount reductions, obviously being quite a notable sort of step down. I noticed your one-off costs were not quite so big in 2025 as 2024.
Just maybe give us a bit of context on where you are in the headcount reduction program, what's left, where are those people actually coming out of? And then the second 1 was just around potential tariff risks across different parts of your business. Perhaps you could give us a little color on that. Thank you.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
On headcount, most of the headcount reduction comes from the factory closures, which is part of the network optimization efforts. That's almost all in Orthopaedics, where we had more capacity than we needed. As part of the broader cost savings programs, we've actually gone after efficiencies right across the group, so significant in SG&A.
Initially, it was as we transitioned into the Business Unit model that was back in 2023. There's actually significant SG&A related headcount savings as well. In 2024, you noted the step up in reduction, if you will. We had to make some difficult decisions there. We've actually pulled forward some of the things we had planned for in 2025 into 2024 as we grappled with the additional headwinds.
Relative to where we started the 12-Point Plan, inflation's been higher for longer, and VBP impact, you know, in sports, which we didn't have at the time we announced the program. Not only in joint repair now coming into AET, has meant we've had to go deeper than we originally set out to do in the 12-Point Plan. The zero-based budgeting approach was 1 of the vehicles we used to get there.
But we've largely done the big bulk of what we set out to do. 25 is the year when the benefits of those actions will flow through into the P&L. That's the headcount, both in terms of where it is and how we're thinking about the phasing or sequence of it.
In terms of tariffs, obviously the headline is it's a dynamic picture, right? It's hard to know how things will actually settle out. When you look at what's been announced so far, you know, this is primarily on China, that is within the realm of what we had contemplated and within the realm of what we expect. Also remind you that tariffs in China is not a new thing.
We've had to navigate that also in the past administration. The topic of reciprocal tariffs and the impact of that, at this point, it's hard to know how that's actually going to play out. The headline for us is we've got a team looking at it.
In terms of the US, the largest proportion of our US business is served through manufacturing plants in the US. We are reasonably well covered there. Where we expect the impact of, to directly answer your question, would be primarily in our wound business, where we've got a significant presence in China in terms of manufacturing.
Having said that, you know, all of our scenario analysis we've done leads us to believe within the realm of the impact will be in the realm of what we expect. The headline again is it's dynamic and it's hard to know how it's gonna play out exactly.
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Just to build for a second on Deepak's comments on the headcount. We're not sort of planning any major sort of headcount reduction plans in 2025 per se. That said, this whole philosophy of ZBB that we've embedded in 2024, we want to make sure it becomes in our DNA and our way of working. As we set our budgets for the 2026 year, you know, we'll be.
We're always looking for opportunity to make ourselves more efficient. There are still opportunities, I believe, in the business where we can drive efficiency through, but it will be done through incremental continuous improvement as opposed to maybe step change on our programs that we've done in 2024.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
John. Question.
Sébastien Jantet
Equity Analyst, Panmure Gordon
Hi, Sébastien Jantet with Panmure Gordon. 2 questions if I can. Just first of all, just wanna talk about pricing a little bit, and just wanna get a sense of what you've baked into your kind of forecast for pricing in some of the major markets, kind of, obviously VBP aside. Secondly, in terms of guidance, you've given yourself quite a big window to drive through for this year.
I'm kind of wondering kind of what are the levers that might leave you at the kind of, you know, the bottom end or top end of that? Is that a revenue outperformance story? Is that cautious guidance on cost savings? Just trying to get a handle on kind of on where we are on that.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
In terms of pricing, you know, historically, we're kind of a 1 to 2% price erosion type of company. It's very fairly typical in the MedTech sector. Over the last couple of years, we've been doing better than that. We've been flat to maybe a percent, a little over a percent up. That's largely because we've been able to pass through our inflation-related cost increases into to our customers.
As you know, in MedTech, historically is not something that you can easily do. What I've commented in the past is we don't expect that to continue out into the future. Our long-term plan basically takes into account going back to normal levels of price erosion, which is around 1 to 2.
Now, we're not gonna get there all in 1 year. We already saw that 2024 was worse. I should use my adjective correctly. Was closer to normal than 2023 was. We expect 2025 to be even closer to normal than that, but not quite at normal, right?
That's the way to think about that process. There's the dynamics in terms of within Orthopaedics, how the mix shift from you know, hospital into ASCs and so forth, and how that plays out. But generally speaking, our long-term plan is based on going back to normal price levels. Before I get to second question, you wanna chime in, John?
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah. Just give you a little bit of color on that. 2024, pricing was roughly, you know, if the group level was up around 1.5% or so, and if you stripped out China, roughly 2%. As Deepak says, elevated levels. For 2025, for the group level, we expect it to be roughly flat, and ex-China would be roughly up 50 basis points. As Deepak says, we're expecting that benefit from price to come off significantly in 2025. That's fully baked in to our forecast and our guidance for the year.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Regarding margin, I wouldn't anchor to either the low end or the high end of that range. The intent here actually is not necessarily to be more conservative on forecasts. I mean, coming off of a margin target that we have in 2025 is not an easily done thing. It was a very painful thing for me personally to have to come off of that.
Having said that, what you also don't wanna do is put forward something and then have to revise it again, right? What we're dealing with is significant uncertainty around China. Bottom line, the reason for this range is China. We've commented on how sports joint repair played out a little differently than we had set out.
The range we've provided takes that into account, but it also takes into account AET, which is the other part of sports that's come through. That range gives us the ability to kind of deliver within that. Like I said, I wouldn't anchor to either the low end or the high end of that range.
As we progress through the year, certainly you know at Q1, we'll be able to kind of tighten up that range for you. Recognizing what John said in his remarks, which is this will be another year where for a variety of reasons, it's gonna be a story of Q2 or H2, kind of margin step up. That's been generally how the last 2 years have played out.
You know, H1 kind of looks kind of ho-hum year on year, and the benefits come through in H2. That's been the story of 2023. It was the story in 2024. The factors have been different in each of those years, but that'll be how 2025 plays out as well.
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah, I mean, if you think about the 3 key levers for margin in 2025 being operational leverage, China effects, cost savings, you know, obviously there's a scenario, you know, if we don't recover US ortho to the extent that we have said we will, that will mean we're at the bottom end of our range. If we do recover or do better, that'll be we're at the top end of our range.
On China, we've baked in 100 basis points of margin dilution, 110 basis points of margin dilution in our bridge. That reflects both the sales reductions that I talked about earlier across both orthopedics and sports. You know, I think we've baked that in, but there's always uncertainty around that, of course. It's very difficult to forecast, but I think we've baked that in. The cost savings.
I feel pretty confident on the cost savings to the degree that, you know, we've got sort of 51 programs that drive those cost savings, half of which are already embedded and complete, the other half of which are close to complete. We've got pretty good visibility of the cost savings. I think in order of risk, you've got the operational leverage piece, then China, and then cost savings where we've got pretty good visibility. The mix of those will determine the bottom and the top end of the range.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
That's great. Thanks, John. 1-2 more questions in the room, and we've got a bunch queued up over the phone. David, and then we'll come back.
David Adlington
Head of European MedTech and Services Research, J.P. Morgan
Thanks. David Adlington from JP Morgan. Just in terms of on the inventory side, maybe for John, any targets you'd be willing to share in terms of how much you might reduce inventory this year? Related to that, how we should be thinking about free cash flow evolving from last year, 'cause last year was obviously very good.
Just on margins, obviously cost savings coming through, getting some top line leverage. How are you thinking about margins beyond 25 and how much you might need to reinvest versus allowing it to drop through?
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Do you want to take the inventory? Look, on inventory, we're not gonna give specific targets. You know, I think we said we've made good progress this year. You've seen it both at group level and more importantly, I think at every single business unit level, we've made good progress on DSI. We also made the point that the quality of our inventory is better.
We've had a buildup of inventory obviously for new product launches, but that's meant that the stuff that doesn't turn very quickly, we've actually reduced the number of those units by about 17%. We're both improving the days sales inventory and also the quality of our inventory.
I think in terms of targets for 2025, we're not gonna be specific on that, but you've seen the direction of travel, and we want to try and maintain that direction of travel through 2025. How does that all impact on our free cash flow? Well, we've said, free cash flow will be north of $600 for the year versus the $551 in 2024. Yeah, I'd like to, you know, I'd like to beat that. I think there's a little bit of a step up in the CapEx as a consequence of our new facility that we're installing in Melton, in Northeast.
I think, you know, we should be aiming to try and be, you know, driving north of $600 and maybe getting to $650 in terms of free cash flow for the year. That should see our leverage reduce from the 1.9 times we exited this year down to 1.6 times at the end of 2025.
That's the direction of travel that we're going in. In terms of margin beyond 2025, you know, look, we're not gonna sit here and give guidance for 2026 and 2027, but we said frequently that, you know, you saw the cost savings come through for this year at $210 over the last 2 years.
We should be trying to get that to close to $300, north of $300, coming through in 2025. We've said $325 to 375 overall, so some of that will come through in 2026 and 2027. Some will be a new savings, some will be annualization of 2025 savings, but we do expect our margin to accrete through 2026 and 2027.
Kane Slutzky
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Morning. Kane Slutzky, Deutsche Bank. Just on robotics, we haven't spoken too much about CORI. I'm just wondering, you've obviously got Mako and ROSA in the large footprint space, but just in the terms of any color you can share on the competitive landscape in the small footprint space where CORI plays, whether it be J&J or TMINI or the other ones.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah, sure.
Kane Slutzky
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Just any sort of commentary there. It sounds like you're gaining some decent momentum.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah. We're first of all very pleased with the traction we're getting with CORI. We're not dissecting the market into small footprint, large footprint. It's the robotics market enables surgeons to implant knees or hips or shoulder. What I'm pleased about is not only the gross number, but where we're actually placing CORI. You know, we're placing them in academic medical institutions where historically we've been under-indexed.
We're placing them in the ASC in a slightly higher proportion than our overall share. You know, speaking to the value proposition, the broad value proposition that CORI has. What I'm also pleased with is the level of utilization. You know, we could be running a place first type of strategy. That's not what we're doing. We're actually placing them where there is demand.
Where we place them, the utilization, you know, is at a nice level. Very pleased with the traction that we're getting. As we indicated since 2022, we've invested in fully featuring CORI. You know, we started out, for example, you know, with a milling-based approach. You know, we got feedback from the market, surgeons' preferences range from cutting and milling.
We brought forward cutting functionality onto CORI, which we had originally not started off with. It's the only platform, and actually, taking a step back, CORI has some features that only it has, right. CORI is the only platform that's able to do revisions because we offer both image and image-free kind of solutions, right?
We are the only platform that's able to do soft tissue balance before the surgeon ever cuts. Each one of these things, you know, aren't on their own gonna move the needle 1 way or another, but the combination is what we're looking for, and it's starting to play itself out that way.
As I commented on around CORI's applicability for shoulder, you know, at the start of the 12-Point Plan, we didn't think about having that program, but we actually pulled it in because we see the potential for the footprint that CORI has. It's not a large installed base, it's a handheld kind of thing. It lends itself to the shoulder space.
We are, on the arthroplasty side, a relatively small player in shoulder, so it's not just about having CORI, but we've got to have a full implant portfolio. As you know, we're on a path, right? We're in the early stages of launch of AETOS shoulder, and that's gonna play itself out. This is a platform that we expect to build on. We've got great proof points already to build on it. Overall, I feel good about how we're positioned competitively within orthopaedics robotics.
Kane Slutzky
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Thanks. John, just maybe a quick 1 for you, just on slide 26 on the ROIC. You're probably not gonna wanna answer this, post-2025, but I mean, you haven't put the numbers in, but it looks as if ortho is doubling its ROIC.
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
That's correct.
Kane Slutzky
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Sorry?
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah.
Kane Slutzky
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Just wondering.
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
We're expecting to double the ROIC in-
Kane Slutzky
Analyst, Deutsche Bank
Yeah, double the ROIC. Assuming obviously you're working your way up to market growth, you haven't fully annualized that number, clearly, but just in 2026, assuming you do get there, should we assume that the ROIC will exceed WACC in post year? Sort of if it doesn't, how long do you give yourselves?
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
I'm not gonna get drawn on when we'll sort of cross the cost of capital line in ortho, but our expectations would suggest it's sometime between 2026 and 2027. We'll see how we progress this year. Certainly a big step up in 2025, so doubling in 2025, and then with a view to getting to our cost of capital sometime in 2026 and 2027.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
The key driver there is US recon performance.
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
What you look for is continued improvement. Obviously we've shown sequential improvement in 2024. We expect to build on that in 2025. That'll be the key kind of lead indicator how we're gonna do on ROIC. We wanna take on the phone. I think we've got Graham Doyle on the phone, we'll get to him first.
Graham Doyle
Analyst, UBS
Thanks, guys. Morning, and thanks for taking the questions. Just 2 for me, 1 on China and 1 on the ortho margin. Just on China, in terms of the, I suppose, the ortho and sports med business, I suspect the question now is there a path where you basically just shut this business down?
Presumably, we're not in margin accretive territory today. Just your thoughts on that and what would be a go, no-go decision. On the plant closure, those are coming through and you're obviously seeing better profits coming through in US ortho in particular. Is there anything we need to think about in terms of the cost of the inventory you hold today and when this kind of better or lower costs inventory comes through?
Just as a sense for us, how much more profitable is US Orthopaedics, given the fixed cost there? Because if we think about the Q4 benefit and the context of the guidance cut in late October and obviously the change there, and then we think about the better momentum continuing to 2025, it's just to get a sense of, like, how much more profitable is this than, say, some of the other businesses that have been growing in the last 2 or 3 years. Thank you very much.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Okay. You were acoustically hard to hear in the second part of the question, so I'll do my best in terms of what I understood it to be. Going to the first thing about China. China Orthopaedics today at VBP price levels is not a profitable business for us. Well, why are we in it?
First, it's giving ourselves the opportunity to see how the market evolves, and in particular how robotics gets adopted in that market. In order for us to do that, you need to maintain a certain level of presence and actually have direct some efforts in developing the robotics market.
Depending on how that develops, China could get back to not what it was in terms of attractiveness from a profitability standpoint, but to a better place than it is today. We're in Orthopaedics today to see how that market actually develops. In sports is a better picture from a profitability standpoint, you know, post the price cut.
I mean, obviously, it is a straight impact to bottom line, right? There is no. Although we've adapted the channel to take VBP pricing into account, it's pretty much a good fall through impact. But it's in a better place than ortho is. That's how to think about the sports business versus the ortho business in China.
In terms of go, no-go decision, we decided to enter into the current round of the recon tender, and that was in March 2024. Originally, it was intended to go for2 years. I mean, there's some indications that they may extend that out to 3 years. The go, no-go decision would be essentially want to participate in the next round of tender, right?
That depends on how the market evolves between now and then. That's the short answer to how we think about go, no-go. In terms of the cost of inventory, as you know, a significant part of the value of the inventory number is from the revaluation of inventory.
It's a fairly complicated picture, but suffice it to say, as we go into 2026 and 2027, as inflation and the impact of inflation recedes, you should start to see what has been a significant headwind turn into a more neutral picture as it comes into our P&L. John, did you catch his question on the 2025 guide?
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
I didn't catch the question, but I just sorta gotta build on the last one. Just on the plant closures, just to be clear.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah.
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
You know, we're already starting to see in cash terms the benefit of those plant closures coming through in terms of our cost of production. As Deepak says, so that's moving in a positive direction. At the moment it's being offset by the inventory revaluation, and hence why the gross margin moved backwards slightly year-over-year, but also the China pricing effects.
Over time, it takes about a year or so in our ortho business for the benefits of those lower production costs to flow through that inventory. That's why we're saying the H2 of this year is when we're gonna see that benefit come through. It's not like we're not enjoying the lower cost today. It just takes about 12 months or so to flow through into the P&L.
That's what gives us pretty good visibility on the numbers as we come through the second half. Just wanna make that point clear. I didn't catch the second question you asked there.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Okay. We need to get to another phone, but Graham is a 30-second kind of repeat of your, the second part of your question.
Graham Doyle
Analyst, UBS
Obviously, that's great, obviously. Thank you very much, guys. Appreciate it.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Thanks, Graham. We go to Hassan from Barclays.
Hassan Al-Wakeel
Head of European MedTech and Services Research, Barclays
Hi, can you hear me?
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
We can.
Hassan Al-Wakeel
Head of European MedTech and Services Research, Barclays
Perfect. Thank you. Hassan Al-Wakeel from Barclays. 3 for me, please. Firstly, just on Q1 and the lower growth here, what could this look like ex China, and how should we think about group growth in Q2, and whether you expect that to be within the guidance range? Just trying to understand how back-end loaded the year is from a growth perspective.
Secondly, related to this on margins, it's not unusual to have 300 basis points of margin differential between H1 and H2, but should we expect a more pronounced difference given the softer H1 growth expectations? Finally, just on the additional VBP in AET, thank you for quantifying. Could you walk us through some of the underlying assumptions in terms of price reduction and volume changes that you've baked in?
What is left in sports medicine in China that hasn't yet had VBP, and how are you thinking about risks here over time? Thank you.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Okay, maybe I'll take the last 1 first and then the next to last, and John, you can take the quarterly phasing. In terms of AET, it's as we indicated in terms of the top line impact. I mean, we called out about $25 million of impact of AET.
It is significantly smaller than our joint repair business. For AET it's a big part, but for a group level, it's not as big a portion. Once VBP gets hit with AET or hits AET, this essentially covers the range of impact to China for the China Sports Medicine business. There's not really a lot left after this. There's a bit of capital, but that's about it.
In terms of the type of margin step up H1 to H2 that we're expecting, what's implied in our models is not an unprecedented level of H1 to H2 margin step up in order to deliver the margin guidance that we've indicated. As you can probably do the math, if you go back to several years in terms of the delta between H1 and H2 margins, what we're expecting in 25 is within kind of the range of what we've seen. You wanna address the quarterly phase?
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Yeah. I'll just come very quickly to the last one. Just on the $25 million that we guided to on AET, that's roughly split. About $15 million of that is price and volume, and about $10 million is channel adjustments. That gives you a little bit of flavor as to the shape of that impact.
The H1, H2 split, I'd look to 2023. That's a good benchmark in terms of the level of step up. In terms of the question around China. If we look at our overall growth ex-China, it is up, you know, obviously there's about 140 BPS of difference for the full year between our ex-China and our group ex-China growth.
China does have quite a big drag on the business. In terms of our ADS growth ex China, we should be looking at around 5% or so for Q1. Q2, we should be looking at around 8% or so, and similar for Q3, and then a little bit of a step down in Q4. It's, again, it's phased through the year, but we are expecting around 4% ADS growth ex China in Q1.
I hope that gives you a bit of color.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Good. I think we'll need to leave it here in the interest of time. I thank you again, for your interest and engagement, and looking forward to coming back in a couple months' time to give you a sense for how, Q1, progressed. Thank you very much.

content.text:
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
Go. Okay, great. Waiting for the safe harbor statement to be read. Good morning, and welcome to the Smith & Nephew Q2 and half year results presentation. I'm Deepak Nath. I'm the Chief Executive Officer, and joining me is Chief Financial Officer John Rogers. I'm pleased to report a solid set of numbers that represents a good step towards our full year guidance and further progress on our strategy to transform Smith & Nephew. On revenue, we delivered the acceleration that we expected with 5.6% growth in the quarter. The Sports Medicine business continued its good momentum across categories and regions. In Advanced Wound Management, we returned to growth with a better quarter in both Bioactives and in AWC. In orthopedics, all of trauma and extremities, robotics, and ex-U.S. Recon have kept performing well, and we've made good progress with addressing our performance in U.S. Recon.
On profitability, 140 basis points of expansion is around the upper end of the guidance range we gave back in May. Operating leverage and our productivity measures in the Twelve-Point Plan more than offset external pressures and have positioned us well to deliver a full year target. It's very encouraging to see double-digit profit growth and also importantly translating into cash with 60% free cash conversion, which is well ahead of where we were last year. My assessment when we began this turnaround was that Smith & Nephew was a portfolio of fundamentally good businesses with excellent technology and the right to win in every part of the company. The diagnosis of why we weren't at full potential was that we had challenges around execution and culture, and we developed the Twelve-Point Plan to address those remaining issues.
The progress we've made since 2022 is evidence that we had the right diagnosis, and we are now firmly on the path to the better financial outcomes that we've been aiming for. The first half of 2024 shows that we're delivering good results from the large majority of the portfolio, making up about 85% of sales. That is a transformation from where we were at the outset, and particularly in Orthopaedics, where we've turned around the majority of the business. Trauma and OUS Recon are now consistently delivering growth well above our history, and CORI has successfully developed from being a new challenger in the market to being recognized as a leading system with strong adoption across a range of settings, from ambulatory surgical care centers to academic medical centers.
It's how we've done all of this that makes me convinced that U.S. Recon is poised to do the same. Firstly, the specific ways we've driven the rest of Orthopaedics are exactly what we're doing in the U.S. We're driving product availability, capital efficiency, and innovation delivery through the various initiatives of the 12-Point Plan. Secondly, we've confirmed the strength of our technology by delivering outperformance with the same products in other markets. Thirdly, I can see the discipline and focus that has come from the 12-Point Plan and our shift to a verticalized, more accountable set of business units. Those benefits apply equally to every part of our portfolio. I'll return to some of these themes later, and John will talk more about cash returns and accountability in his presentation. For now, I'll take you through the detail of the quarter.
Revenue in the quarter was $1.4 billion with 5.6% underlying growth and 4.6% reported, with 100 basis points headwind from foreign exchange. Growth also included a tailwind from one more trading day than in the prior year. All three business units accelerated sequentially, and I'll come to the detail in a moment. Geographically, the U.S. grew at 3.6%, and other established markets grew 6.9%. Emerging markets grew at 9.5%, with strong double-digit growth across the Middle East, India, and Latin America. For the business unit performance, I'll start with Orthopaedics, which grew at 5.8% underlying. Global knees and hips grew by 2.1% and 4.4% respectively. The geographic trends in recent quarters continued with higher growth in the OUS segment, particularly in Europe.
Almost half of our recon business is in those international markets where we're demonstrating what our portfolio can deliver with good execution. Even as we of course lap stronger comps, U.S. Recon was still behind for the quarter as a whole, but there were encouraging signs of progress. Our operational improvements under the 12-Point Plan are now at goal, with both implant supply and now set availability at target levels. That's for both hips and knees as well. We're also seeing indicators of commercial effectiveness moving favorably, particularly around staff retention. Other recon grew 17.8% and reflects another good quarter of robotics placements, particularly in the U.S. We've also continued to develop our offering with the launch in June of the CORI pre-operative planning and modeling.
The launch makes CORI the only robotics system to offer a choice of imagery and image-based planning, and is another element in our approach of supporting a range of surgeon preferences on a single platform. Trauma and extremities grew 11.8%, providing half of the overall Orthopaedics growth. The EVOS plating system continues to be a key driver within core trauma, and the growth contribution of AETOS shoulder is steadily increasing as we deploy more capital and convert new surgeons. Sports Medicine and ENT grew 7.6% in the quarter. Within that, joint repair growth was 6%, including the expected headwind from volume-based procurement in China. While the implementation began only in May, we saw ordering patterns affected for the whole of Q2. Excluding China, joint repair growth would have been 11.8%, with a very strong quarter across our other major markets.
By product, the knee repair portfolio and REGENETEN were again key contributors, and we're well advanced with the post-acquisition integration of CartiHeal AGILI-C. That's one of our next generation growth drivers. Early cohorts of sales reps have completed the training, and we're starting to build out patient and surgeon access. Arthroscopic enabling technologies grew by 8.7%. Higher growth in the quarter came from the expected recovery in video capital sales and continued good performance from our radio frequency platform, both from core ablation and from wearable FASTSEAL. ENT revenue growth of 11.6% was driven by our core tonsil and adenoid business. While underlying demand continues to grow well, I'd remind you that the next quarter will have a very strong prior year comparator with the effect that the ENT growth in Q3 is likely to be around flat.

We’re in a good place in terms of leadership there. We’ve been able to attract actually good talent across the industry into our organization because people are attracted by our product portfolio. We’ve got great products in Recon. Yes, our share position doesn’t reflect it. If you’re a patient, if you’re a surgeon, you know how good our products are, and our reps see that.
We've been able to recruit good reps. Finally, on the compensation scheme, we've rolled that out, right. As I've indicated, in 2022, we're really largely up until that point, operating in a mode of retention-based schemes. Now, there are good reasons for that. It's because historically we've had challenges retaining the business for product availability reasons, product portfolio gap reasons, and other things. There's a challenge around even retaining business. We're now with all of those things largely at hand. We're able to be much more front-footed, and we've got an incentive scheme that rewards that. Not everybody's going to like that, right? We expect that, but it's now been, you know, rolled out, and people understand what they need to do to earn their quota.
That is all at hand. In terms of procedures, I've commented in the past that in recon, because we've had performance challenges of our own, I don't tend to comment independently with our own data on how we're doing. We see all of the datasets in the industry that everybody else does, right? When you have performance challenge in that business, it can be hard to parse what's market and what's you. We can do that very well in our other businesses, in sports and other things. We have a pretty good view of what's happening in the market. In ortho, and particularly in recon, I've been somewhat circumspect about commenting on what's actually happening in the market independent of what we all see with other companies reporting.
What I can say with that proviso is the market seems pretty robust, you know, back to more normalized levels. We clearly saw in Q1 and Q2 of last year a very frothy market. We're not in that world right now. We're in a more normalized world. For us, our assumptions as far as the guidance that we gave assumed a normalized market. We're not counting on a market tailwind to deliver our numbers. Hopefully, it gives you the color around this. Not as straightforward an answer as you might like, but at least you know our thought process there.
John Rogers
CFO, Smith & Nephew
Just on your question around the phasing of savings. The chart shows, as you know, accumulated savings over time on a 2023 base. As you rightly highlight, there's a big assumed step-up in 2025 versus 2024. That shouldn't obviously be a surprise to you because our margin guidance for 25 is north of 20%, and our margin guidance for 24 is north of 18%. That's what it takes to get to our 20%. The reason for that phasing is, you know, a lot of the savings that we're forecasting to come through from manufacturing; we see a big step up. Actually, if you look at the chart and you unpick the detail, it's really across all areas.
As we start to implement these initiatives, deliver, we get sort of some within-year effects in the first year, and then we get a full annualisation in the second year, and then they build. That's really explaining the nature of these savings coming through and the timing. I think you also asked a question about beyond 2025, and again, you can see there's a little bit of further coming through in 2025 and 2026, which all else being equal, obviously helps margin in those years. As I said, what I don't want to happen is for this to translate into any form of indications as to where margins will be in 2026 and 2027. There's a lot of time between now and then, a lot of moving parts, and we'll come back to that obviously in due course.
The one thing I would want to make clear, you know, we said, you know, all along that the 25 margin target, you know, is challenging, you know. It is challenging because of all the reasons we've talked about. You know, we've got the inflationary headwinds, and they've been perhaps a little bit stickier than we first envisaged. We've got the China VBP, which, you know, came out post us providing this target range. We've had to necessarily get into the business, get into the detail, look at the 12-Point Plan, and we've been able to identify these additional savings, which help us offset some of those headwinds and challenges. The target for 25 remains challenging. We're confident in reiterating the guidance today of north of 20%.
Deepak Nath
CEO, Smith & Nephew
I think with that, I understand we're at time. Wanted on behalf of John, myself, and the management team, thank you very much for your attention and engagement, and look forward to coming back to you next quarter, reporting on progress. Thank you. Bye-bye.
